In 2013 SNAP helped more than 47 million Americans afford a nutri-
tionally adequate diet in a typical month. It also kept about 4.9 million 
people out of poverty in 2012, including 1.3 million children (Center on 
Budget and Policy Priorities, 2015). A recent study has shown that after 
these expansions in the 1960s and 1970s, disadvantaged children with 
access to nutrition assistance in early childhood and who had mothers 
that received assistance during pregnancy, had improved health and 
education outcomes, better growth curves, and fewer diagnoses of 
heart disease and obesity (Hoynes et al, 2012). Today, state agencies 
administering SNAP have the option of providing nutrition education to 
SNAP participants through federal grants and matching fund programs 
(USDA, 2015).
